## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

7	
8	The owner adds articles so the project can keep working **without reopening them**. An intake is

15	## The steps
16	
17	### 1. Place the paper
18	
19	Slug is `<first-author>-<year>-<short-topic>`. Create `references/<slug>/` and `git mv` the PDF in
20	as `<slug>.pdf` — the original file keeps its content but not its unwieldy download name.

22	### 2. Extract text and images
23	
24	```
25	python3 references/_tools/extract_pdf_assets.py references/<slug>/<slug>.pdf /tmp/<slug>
26	```
27	
28	Writes `fulltext.txt`, `raw/` and `manifest.tsv`. **Work from the scratchpad**, not the repo —
29	only named, described figures get committed.
30	
31	### 3. Chase the supplementary material — it is often where the method actually lives
32	
33	**Ask for it if it is not to hand.** Rust 2020's main text leaves the binarization method, the
34	filter radius, the particle-size floor and the heatmap grid all unstated; its supplementary Data
35	Sheet supplied every one of them, plus the verbatim macro and a **µm-calibrated native-resolution
36	vessel image** that became the best input in the repo and the basis of the strongest validation
37	the project has. That material was one download away and the digest was materially wrong without it.
38	
39	Commit supplementary code, scripts, LUTs and data images under
40	`references/<slug>/supplementary/`. Transcribe supplementary *tables* into the digest.
41	
42	### 4. Read the whole paper
43	
44	Read `fulltext.txt` end to end. Then **look at every extracted image** — do not skip this. Papers
45	put their method in figures: Rust 2020's entire pipeline specification exists only as pixels in
46	Figure 1C. Anything that is only in an image and matters must be **transcribed into the digest**.
47	
48	### 5. Name and commit the figures
49	
50	`git mv` each real figure to `references/<slug>/figures/figN_<short-name>.png` (convert to PNG).
51	Drop logos, glyphs and icons. Write `figures/README.md`: every figure **shown inline**
52	(`![Figure 1](fig1_….png)`) with a description of each sub-panel, what the scale bars say, and
53	**what you actually see in it** — including anything that will trip the pipeline up (surface
54	vessels, drawn annotation lines, cross-sections rather than networks).
55	
56	### 6. Crop the panels
57	
58	Locate the grid programmatically where possible (photomicrograph panels are dark, the page is
59	white — find the dark bands), then **freeze the coordinates** into
60	`references/<slug>/figures/crop_panels.py` so the crop is reproducible. Prefix the isolated
61	vessel-channel panels `VESSEL_` and nothing else. Tag every panel name with the paper
62	(`rust20fig1_…`) so calibration prefixes stay unique. Write `figures/panels/README.md`: the
63	inventory, the µm/px per row, and the caveats that come with folding these into the dataset.
64	
65	### 7. Calibrate — measure, never assume
66	
67	**Measure the drawn scale bar in pixels off the panel itself** and add the prefix to
68	`SCALEBAR_PX` in `analysis/measure_vessels.py` (plus `SCALEBAR_UM` if the bar is not 50 µm).
69	Never derive µm/px from a stated field-of-view, and never carry a number over from a
70	neighbouring row.
71	
72	If the source image **states its own µm/px** (an ImageJ TIFF carries `unit=` and `XResolution`),
73	use that instead and record it in `UMPP_DIRECT` with its provenance — acquisition metadata is
74	better evidence than a bar measured off a printed page. **Cross-check it against biology** before
75	trusting it: capillaries should come out at roughly 4–8 µm across.
76	
77	If a figure draws **no** bar, put the prefix in `UNCALIBRATED` **with the reason**. That panel
78	then reports area % and pixels only. All three tables are checked by `panel-scale-calibration`.
79	
80	Cross-check when the figure lets you: a close-up's ROI box in its overview gives an independent
81	magnification estimate. **Record the agreement, and record it when it is poor** — that is a real
82	uncertainty in every length the panel produces.
83	
84	### 8. Write the digest
85	
86	`references/<slug>/digest.md`. It must stand alone. Always include:
87	
88	- **Citation block** — title, authors, venue, DOI, licence, link to the PDF, one-line thesis.
89	- **§ Why this matters to *our* task** — first, and concrete. What does this paper change about
90	  what we build? What does it explicitly *not* cover?
91	- **The method, in full.** Every parameter the paper states. Every parameter it *fails* to state,
92	  listed as a gap, so nobody re-hunts.
93	- **The reported numbers**, in tables, with the stats.
94	- **Calibration facts** for the extracted panels, with the caveats from step 7.
95	- **Discussion arguments worth keeping**, and the authors' own stated limitations.
96	- **§ What is not in this PDF** — supplementary material, scripts, anything you tried to fetch and
97	  could not (record the URL and what happened).
98	- **§ Extracted images** — the figure table, linked.
99	
100	### 9. Fold into the synthesis
101	
102	Update [`references/METHODS-SYNTHESIS.md`](../../../../../../references/METHODS-SYNTHESIS.md): add
103	the paper to the folded-in list, extend the metric and processing tables, add reference
104	magnitudes, and — most valuable — **compare the published numbers to ours and say what the gap
105	means**. A published branch density 5× below ours is a sharper statement of our fragmentation
106	problem than any overlay.
107	
108	Add the paper's row to [`references/README.md`](../../../../../../references/README.md).
109	
110	### 10. Verify
111	
112	```
113	python3 analysis/measure_vessels.py                                   # new panels appear, µm sane
114	node .claudinite/local/packs/vascular-coloring/pack.test.mjs          # checks still pass
115	```

118	
119	- **Never invent a number.** Not a scale bar, not a field size, not a metric. Measure it, cite it,
120	  or declare it unknown. This is the project's first rule and intake is where it is most tempting
121	  to break.
122	- **The pipeline's own output is never ground truth** for a new panel set. A digest may quote what
123	  the *authors* measured; it must not present our run over their images as validation.
124	- **Say what is weak.** A calibration you half-trust, a panel type the metrics do not suit, a
125	  direction-of-change that contradicts another paper — all of it goes in the digest. The digests
126	  are read later by someone deciding what to believe.
127	- **Different papers are never averaged together.** Species, model, marker and magnification all
128	  differ; the rollup is grouped per paper for that reason.
129	- **Prefer a same-image comparison to a table comparison.** If the paper ships code *and* an
130	  image, reimplement the method and run both on that image. Comparing our figure-crop output to a
131	  published summary table produced a confident, wrong conclusion about our branch counts; running
132	  the authors' own macro on their own image corrected it. A number from a summary table may not
133	  be the raw output of the method it describes.

Figure 1C. Anything that is only in an image and matters must be **transcribed into the digest**.

### 5. Name and commit the figures

`git mv` each real figure to `references/<slug>/figures/figN_<short-name>.png` (convert to PNG).
Drop logos, glyphs and icons. Write `figures/README.md`: every figure **shown inline**
(`![Figure 1](fig1_….png)`) with a description of each sub-panel, what the scale bars say, and
**what you actually see in it** — including anything that will trip the pipeline up (surface
vessels, drawn annotation lines, cross-sections rather than networks).

### 6. Crop the panels

Locate the grid programmatically where possible (photomicrograph panels are dark, the page is
white — find the dark bands), then **freeze the coordinates** into
`references/<slug>/figures/crop_panels.py` so the crop is reproducible. Prefix the isolated
vessel-channel panels `VESSEL_` and nothing else. Tag every panel name with the paper
(`rust20fig1_…`) so calibration prefixes stay unique. Write `figures/panels/README.md`: the
inventory, the µm/px per row, and the caveats that come with folding these into the dataset.

### 7. Calibrate — measure, never assume

**Measure the drawn scale bar in pixels off the panel itself** and add the prefix to
`SCALEBAR_PX` in `analysis/measure_vessels.py` (plus `SCALEBAR_UM` if the bar is not 50 µm).
Never derive µm/px from a stated field-of-view, and never carry a number over from a
neighbouring row.

If the source image **states its own µm/px** (an ImageJ TIFF carries `unit=` and `XResolution`),
use that instead and record it in `UMPP_DIRECT` with its provenance — acquisition metadata is
better evidence than a bar measured off a printed page. **Cross-check it against biology** before
trusting it: capillaries should come out at roughly 4–8 µm across.

If a figure draws **no** bar, put the prefix in `UNCALIBRATED` **with the reason**. That panel
then reports area % and pixels only. All three tables are checked by `panel-scale-calibration`.

Cross-check when the figure lets you: a close-up's ROI box in its overview gives an independent
magnification estimate. **Record the agreement, and record it when it is poor** — that is a real
uncertainty in every length the panel produces.

### 8. Write the digest

`references/<slug>/digest.md`. It must stand alone. Always include:

- **Citation block** — title, authors, venue, DOI, licence, link to the PDF, one-line thesis.
- **§ Why this matters to *our* task** — first, and concrete. What does this paper change about
  what we build? What does it explicitly *not* cover?
- **The method, in full.** Every parameter the paper states. Every parameter it *fails* to state,
  listed as a gap, so nobody re-hunts.
- **The reported numbers**, in tables, with the stats.
- **Calibration facts** for the extracted panels, with the caveats from step 7.
- **Discussion arguments worth keeping**, and the authors' own stated limitations.
- **§ What is not in this PDF** — supplementary material, scripts, anything you tried to fetch and
  could not (record the URL and what happened).
- **§ Extracted images** — the figure table, linked.

### 9. Fold into the synthesis

Update [`references/METHODS-SYNTHESIS.md`](../../../../../../references/METHODS-SYNTHESIS.md): add
the paper to the folded-in list, extend the metric and processing tables, add reference
magnitudes, and — most valuable — **compare the published numbers to ours and say what the gap
means**. A published branch density 5× below ours is a sharper statement of our fragmentation
problem than any overlay.

Add the paper's row to [`references/README.md`](../../../../../../references/README.md).

### 10. Verify

```
python3 analysis/measure_vessels.py                                   # new panels appear, µm sane
node .claudinite/local/packs/vascular-coloring/pack.test.mjs          # checks still pass
```

## The rules that bite here

- **Never invent a number.** Not a scale bar, not a field size, not a metric. Measure it, cite it,
  or declare it unknown. This is the project's first rule and intake is where it is most tempting
  to break.
- **The pipeline's own output is never ground truth** for a new panel set. A digest may quote what
  the *authors* measured; it must not present our run over their images as validation.
- **Say what is weak.** A calibration you half-trust, a panel type the metrics do not suit, a
  direction-of-change that contradicts another paper — all of it goes in the digest. The digests
  are read later by someone deciding what to believe.
- **Different papers are never averaged together.** Species, model, marker and magnification all
  differ; the rollup is grouped per paper for that reason.
- **Prefer a same-image comparison to a table comparison.** If the paper ships code *and* an
  image, reimplement the method and run both on that image. Comparing our figure-crop output to a
  published summary table produced a confident, wrong conclusion about our branch counts; running
  the authors' own macro on their own image corrected it. A number from a summary table may not
  be the raw output of the method it describes.

name: vessel-overlay-review
description: Show a vessel-extraction result as an annotated overlay on the original panel and state explicit visual assertions about it. Use whenever proposing, revising, or reporting on the segmentation/measurement pipeline in this repo — before quoting any new numbers.
---

# Reviewing a vessel extraction on the overlay

The owner reacts to **pictures with claims attached**, not to metric tables. Any change to
`analysis/measure_vessels.py` (segmentation, pruning, branch graph, caliber threshold) is presented
this way before its numbers are quoted.

## 1. Regenerate

```
python3 analysis/measure_vessels.py                  # per-image + region metrics table
python3 analysis/annotate_overlays.py [name-substr]  # presentation overlays -> analysis/annotated/
```

Both output directories hold renders, not data: regenerate them, never commit their PNGs
(`render-outputs-gitignored` keeps every render directory ignored by git,
`rendered-overlays-untracked` catches a PNG that got committed anyway). Setup:
`pip install -r requirements.txt`.

## 2. Keep the agreed overlay style

`analysis/annotate_overlays.py` is the source of truth for it, and it is the style the owner
iterated to — change it only on request:

- overlay on the **original at full brightness**; the debug 3-panel view in `measure_vessels.py`
  (`--overlays`) may dim, the presentation overlay may not;
- a highlight is a **slim outline that circles the thing — never a colour fill**; contours drawn at
  display resolution, 1 px, alpha-blended so the signal reads through;
- colours contrast with the red channel — cyan capillary, green artery, magenta junction, yellow
  labels. **No red overlay marks** (`overlay-color-contrast` enforces this);
- arrows label representative vessels with their length in µm, one artery with its diameter; a drawn
  50 µm bar and a totals banner (segments cap/artery, length + density, junctions, area %).

## 3. State the assertions

Alongside the overlay, write the claims a reader can check against it, in both directions:

- **what the method caught** — "each cyan outline is one segment I counted";
- **what it missed or broke** — "the red vessel at lower-left carries no outline: under-detection in
  this dim field"; "this vessel is split into three segments by a stain dropout, so COUNT is
  inflated here".

Compare against the visual expectations in
`references/wang-2022-cd31-vascular-network/figures/panels/expected-results.md` — never against the pipeline's own previous output.

## 4. Then the numbers

Use **length density / area %** for anything cross-figure (the
figures are at different zoom). Record the accepted change and its metric delta in
`analysis/results-first-pass.md`, and refresh `analysis/STATUS.md`'s "trustworthy vs not" and next
step so the next session resumes from it.

2	// An issue titled `[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task> [qualifier]`, whose labels are
3	// its state, whose body's first line is the task path, and whose optional body
4	// fields (`Not-before`, `Blocked-by`, and a request's `Request` / `Model`) are the
5	// only facts it carries beyond that.
6	//
7	// PURE, and deliberately the whole schema: everything else — anchors, guards,
8	// yields, leashes, verdicts — is computed fresh at every scheduler run and pick from the
9	// engine and the declarations at HEAD (DESIGN §14). The label-and-field vocabulary
10	// here is therefore the compatibility surface across engine versions, which is why
11	// additive change is the strongly preferred shape and a rename needs a migration.
12	//
13	// Parse/serialize of those fields lives here and nowhere else (DESIGN §9).
14	//
15	// The one import, and a frozen constant at that: the pack-rename map, which this
16	// module needs to keep reading titles written before a rename (see parseWorkItemTitle).
17	import { canonicalPackId } from '../../pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs';
18	
19	// The title prefix. Disjoint from the slot mechanism's `[claudinite-task]` on
20	// purpose: the two mechanisms coexist per-repo behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`,
21	// and neither may read the other's issues (DESIGN §14, S29).
22	export const WORK_PREFIX = '[claudinite-work]';
23	
24	// --- the canonical vocabulary (DESIGN §4, the migration of #1119) -------------
25	// Every label the machinery writes is one of three things — the item's single
26	// STATUS, its lifelong ORIGIN, or the URGENCY flag — and all of them live in the
27	// `task:` namespace. These are the spellings a reader compares against: decode
28	// first (`statusOf`, `originOf`), then compare, so an item filed by any engine
29	// version answers the same question the same way.
30	export const STATUS_PREFIX = 'task:status:';
31	export const PARK_PREFIX = `${STATUS_PREFIX}needs-human-`;
32	
33	export const STATUS_BLOCKED = `${STATUS_PREFIX}blocked`;
34	export const STATUS_READY = `${STATUS_PREFIX}waiting-for-executor`;
35	export const STATUS_RUNNING_EXECUTOR = `${STATUS_PREFIX}running-executor`;
36	export const STATUS_RUNNING_AGENT = `${STATUS_PREFIX}running-agent`;
37	export const STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_ACTION = `${PARK_PREFIX}action`;
38	export const STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_DECISION = `${PARK_PREFIX}decision`;
39	export const STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_APPROVAL = `${PARK_PREFIX}approval`;
40	export const STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_FAILURE = `${PARK_PREFIX}failure`;
41	export const STATUS_DONE = `${STATUS_PREFIX}done`;
42	export const STATUS_REJECTED = `${STATUS_PREFIX}rejected`;
43	
44	// The four statuses an OPEN item may wear before it parks or converges. An open
45	// item wearing no decodable status at all is off the state machine — a torn label
46	// swap's leavings, which the janitor repairs (DESIGN §6.2, §11).
47	export const LIVE_STATUSES = Object.freeze([
48	  STATUS_BLOCKED, STATUS_READY, STATUS_RUNNING_EXECUTOR, STATUS_RUNNING_AGENT,
49	]);
50	// The park kinds, in the order a decoder prefers them when an item somehow wears
51	// more than one: `failure` first, because it is the conservative lane — the one
52	// that holds the task's lane rather than letting a broken task keep filing work.
53	export const PARK_KINDS = Object.freeze(['failure', 'action', 'decision', 'approval']);
54	export const PARK_STATUSES = Object.freeze(PARK_KINDS.map((k) => `${PARK_PREFIX}${k}`));
55	export const STATUS_LABELS = Object.freeze([
56	  ...LIVE_STATUSES, ...PARK_STATUSES, STATUS_DONE, STATUS_REJECTED,
57	]);
58	
59	// THE ORIGIN (DESIGN §3, decision §15.29) — who asked for this item, worn for the
60	// item's whole life beside whatever status it holds. Read here; the writers arrive
61	// with the write-side flip.
62	export const ORIGIN_PREFIX = 'task:origin:';
63	export const ORIGIN_PLANNED = `${ORIGIN_PREFIX}planned`;
64	export const ORIGIN_AD_HOC = `${ORIGIN_PREFIX}ad-hoc`;
65	export const ORIGIN_GITHUB = `${ORIGIN_PREFIX}github`;
66	export const ORIGIN_LABELS = Object.freeze([ORIGIN_PLANNED, ORIGIN_AD_HOC, ORIGIN_GITHUB]);
67	
68	// --- the write spellings ------------------------------------------------------
69	// What this engine APPLIES. They are separate from the canonical constants above
70	// for the length of the migration only: reads decode every spelling, writes carry
71	// one, and the flip is these six values changing (#1119).
72	export const BLOCKED = 'task:blocked';
73	export const READY = 'task:ready';
74	export const URGENT = 'task:urgent';
75	export const EXECUTING = 'task:executing';
76	export const AGENT = 'task:agent';
77	export const NEEDS_HUMAN = 'needs-human';
78	
79	// @deprecated Nothing writes this since the approval park: a run that left an
80	// unmerged PR no longer CLOSES as delivered, it parks at
81	// `task:needs-human-approval` and waits to be merged. Kept exported, kept in
82	// `QUEUE_LABELS`, and still read everywhere it was read — closed issues carrying
83	// it are stored data, and a decoder that stopped recognising it would turn every
84	// historical delivered run into an un-outcomed one.
85	export const OUTCOME_DELIVERED = 'outcome:delivered';
86	
87	// @deprecated The pre-2026-08-19 spellings of the two terminals below. Kept
88	// exported so a fielded pack that imports them still loads, and READ wherever an
89	// outcome is decoded: labels are stored data on closed issues fleet-wide, so a
90	// decoder that stopped recognising these would turn every historical run into an
91	// un-outcomed one. Write `TASK_DONE` / `TASK_OBSOLETE`.
92	export const OUTCOME_DONE = 'outcome:done';
93	export const OUTCOME_OBSOLETE = 'outcome:obsolete';
94	
95	// Today's terminal spellings (DESIGN §4, §15.25): the `outcome:` namespace dissolves
96	// into `task:`, one vocabulary for the state machine's live and terminal states
97	// alike. These are what the engine WRITES; the `outcome:*` spellings above are read
98	// forever, because a closed issue keeps whatever it was closed under.

100	export const TASK_OBSOLETE = 'task:obsolete';
101	
102	// @deprecated The origin marker (DESIGN §15.26). Nothing writes it and nothing
103	// branches on it: whether an item is a task's standing occurrence or an ad-hoc run
104	// is STRUCTURAL — see `isStandingItem` — so a marker that could disagree with the
105	// structure was a second authority over the same fact. Kept exported and inert
106	// because open items filed by an older engine still carry it, and a reader that
107	// choked on an unknown label would fail on exactly those.
108	export const ORIGIN_SCHEDULE = 'origin:schedule';

111	// human parked with it is expected to DO, which is the whole difference between a
112	// queue a person can skim and one they have to read. Every park wears BOTH:

117	//   action   — something outside the code must change: a secret set, a scope

127	// `failure` is the default a park falls back to, so an unclassified park reads as

132	export const NEEDS_HUMAN_APPROVAL = triage('approval');
133	export const NEEDS_HUMAN_FAILURE = triage('failure');

This session was dispatched via the queue (`.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/invoke.mjs`) to work item #159 (`claudinite-growth/rule-revalidation`). `queue/instructions.md` step 6 says to converge with:

```
node <engine>/scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs --issue <n> --outcome ... --summary ...
```

That script (`converge-item.mjs` → `signals/gh.mjs`'s `makeGh()`) reads and writes the issue over a direct `fetch` against `api.github.com`, authenticated with `process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN`. Run from this session it fails two ways in sequence:

1. Without `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` set (never set in this session type), it exits immediately: `converge-item: GITHUB_REPOSITORY is not set`.
2. Exporting `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` and retrying, the read call itself comes back `403`: `GitHub access is not enabled for this session. An org admin must connect the Claude GitHub App for this organization.`

This matches what this session's own instructions state plainly: it has no `gh` CLI and no direct GitHub API access, only the GitHub MCP connector — the same fact `engine/scheduler/executor.md` documents for the retired slot mechanism ("GitHub access is MCP-only — this session carries no repo token, so every read and write goes through your GitHub tools"), but which `queue/instructions.md` and `converge-item.mjs` do not account for.

**Impact:** a session dispatched this way (a Claude Code cloud/web session, as opposed to a GitHub Actions runner) cannot run the mandated convergence script at all. I did not attempt to hand-roll the label transition instead — `converge-item.mjs`'s own design rationale, and `github.mjs`'s explicit rule that label writes must stay granular (add/remove one named label, never write the label set, to avoid clobbering a concurrent transition), both argue against reconstructing this by hand from a different session. The only MCP tool available for issue labels (`issue_write`) has a `labels` field of unconfirmed replace-vs-add semantics, which is exactly the hazard that rule exists to avoid guessing at.

**This is a canon-side gap** (`converge-item.mjs` and `signals/gh.mjs` live under the vendored `.claudinite/shared/` tree, which this repo never hand-edits), not something fixable from this repo. A human should either give `converge-item.mjs` an MCP-backed transport option for sessions of this type, or make `queue/instructions.md` name a converge path that works from a queue-dispatched Claude Code session rather than assuming a GitHub Actions runner's token.
